Gary Grigsby’s War in the East is a monumental operational-level World War II wargame that stands as one of the most detailed and demanding strategy simulations ever released on Steam. Developed by 2by3 Games and published by Matrix Games, the game focuses entirely on the Eastern Front conflict between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, spanning from the opening stages of Operation Barbarossa in 1941 through the final collapse of German forces in 1945. Rather than offering a streamlined or cinematic interpretation of history, the game commits to a near-academic level of simulation, presenting warfare as a vast, exhausting contest of logistics, manpower, terrain, weather, and long-term planning. From the very first turn, it makes clear that this is not a casual strategy title but a deep, uncompromising war simulation designed for players who want to engage with history at a granular operational scale.

The scope of War in the East is staggering. The map stretches across thousands of hexes, covering nearly the entire Eastern European theater, with each hex representing roughly ten miles of terrain and each turn equating to a week of real time. Players command thousands of units at the division and brigade level, managing armies that can number in the millions of soldiers. Movement, combat, and positioning all require careful consideration, as even small mistakes can cascade into large-scale disasters weeks later. Unlike many strategy games that reward constant aggression, War in the East emphasizes patience and realism; overextending forces, neglecting supply lines, or ignoring seasonal weather effects can cripple even the strongest offensives. Every decision feels heavy, and the long campaign structure ensures that early choices echo far into the future.

One of the defining strengths of the game is its logistics and supply system, which plays a central role in shaping the entire experience. Armies do not simply advance because they have strong units; they advance only if rail networks are repaired, supply depots are functioning, and fuel and ammunition can reach the front lines. This creates a constant tension between ambition and practicality, especially for the German side, which must balance rapid advances against the risk of logistical collapse. Weather further complicates matters, with mud seasons and harsh winters dramatically reducing movement and combat effectiveness, often forcing players to pause or regroup at historically accurate moments. These systems combine to create a simulation that feels authentic and punishing in equal measure, reinforcing the idea that victory is earned through preparation as much as battlefield success.

The presentation of War in the East is functional rather than inviting, reflecting its priorities. The interface is dense with information, tables, and nested menus, and while everything is there for a reason, it can be overwhelming to new players. Learning how to interpret combat odds, unit readiness, morale, and supply status requires time and patience, and the game’s infamous manual is often as challenging as the game itself. However, for those willing to invest the effort, the clarity of information eventually becomes a strength, allowing experienced players to make informed, deliberate decisions based on a wealth of data. This learning curve is steep, but it is also part of the game’s identity, rewarding dedication with a level of strategic control rarely found elsewhere.

Single-player campaigns offer a formidable challenge, with AI opponents capable of mounting credible offensives and defensive operations across the massive map. However, the game truly shines in multiplayer, particularly through its play-by-email system, where two human commanders can wage a campaign over months or even years of real time. Facing another player introduces unpredictability and psychological warfare that elevate the experience beyond scripted behavior, turning each campaign into a unique historical what-if scenario. These long-form matches capture the exhausting, attritional nature of the Eastern Front better than almost any other digital game, as both sides slowly adapt, counter, and exploit weaknesses over hundreds of turns.

Ultimately, Gary Grigsby’s War in the East is not a game that tries to appeal to everyone, nor does it need to. It is a definitive, uncompromising simulation aimed squarely at dedicated wargame enthusiasts and history buffs who appreciate complexity, realism, and long-term strategic thinking. Its age shows in its interface and presentation, but its systems remain remarkably deep and relevant, even years after release. For players willing to commit the time and mental energy required to master its mechanics, the game offers an unparalleled portrayal of the largest land war in human history, delivering a sense of scale, consequence, and historical immersion that few strategy titles have ever matched.

Decades ago, when I was young I had a copy of SPI's monster board game, War in the East. It had, I believe 7 maps and a couple thousand counters and they were all spread out on my living room floor for months whilst I enjoyed myself. Well, SPI went out of business in the early 80s, but some years ago Decision Games published a PC version of the game, War in Europe. 

War in Europe was a divisional level representation of WWII, with a big rule book and an intricate production system. Originally for the Soviets in War in the East and then expanded to the Germans and Allies for War in Europe, the players not only controlled how and where their armies moved, but decided what units to produce, how fast, and when to produce them. It was a huge, intricate game and I really enjoyed it.

So when I saw Gary Grigsby's War in the East a few years ago, I figured it was a similar type of game. In some respects that is true -- in fact, this game goes even further internally, taking the simulation detail down to individual weapons and machines. This game has a detailed production system that covers basically everything that goes into your army and air forces. I was initially put off by all the screens of production data. However, as I got further into it, I realized that all this was totally handled by the game -- the player can pretty much view the production system as a black box, from which tanks and rifle squads emerge.

The game map is definitely big -- 10 mile hexes, and the basic units are divisions and air bases. The game models a chain of command, starting from OKH or Stavka, going down through army groups, armies, corps, and finally divisions. There is a detailed supply system, where supply also flows down from the railroads to corps to divisions. There are commanders at corps level and above. Various aspects of the air war are modeled as well.

So what I've been learning, especially lately, is that you, the player, can make use of all these systems and really get down into the weeds and control to at least some extend most of the variables in the game outside of production. If you are a detail freak or control fanatic, you can probably spend hours getting every aspect of your army 'just so' for each turn.

On the other hand, you don't have to do all that. You have a lot of fun just moving your units around, attacking, setting up defensive lines, etc. The game will do a decent job of handling all the other stuff behind the curtain and let you concentrate on strategy and tactics. There's nothing wrong with this approach, and it's probably a good way to get into the game.

There is also a middle road. Without getting extremely detailed, you can lift the curtain a bit and make intelligent use of some of the mechanics without going overboard. Some things like making sure your combat divisions are always within supply range of their corps, replacing bad commanders with better one, rotating units out of the front lines when they get fatigued or depleted. There are a lot of things you can improve on without obsessing too much over. This is one reason I think this is a very good war game.

This is for serious 'grognards' only - those who delight in researching and recreating the hundreds of battles in WW2. This is needlessly complex to allow the player to squad out generals, set the various plane squadrons to either bombing or air defense, you must maintain chain of supply to headquarter units which gets tedious real fast. I grew up playing the board games this is based off of (Victory Games like Pacific War, 6th Fleet, Avalon Hill's Squad Leader, etc.). I can beat Panzer General on medium difficulty. I find this game frustrating because it seems to be designed like real life - nearly impossible to beat. I have played the most "simple" scenario Road to Minsk 10 times and can beat it only on the Easiest difficulty, and even then only achieve a minor victory. Turn times are 30 to 60 seconds (staring at the screen and waiting). I have to set certain things every turn because the game resets them and there's no way to set them on by default (shift-z to view HQ links; victory condition flags). There are few tutorials on the web and those available only show easy difficulty victories because there's probably no one that can beat them on challenging. While that makes it like real life it doesn't make for a fun game, at least for me. The manual is over 300 pages long in 8-point font text. And it's the most expensive game on steam ($80 without DLC!). Military historians who know the caliber of weapons used on every vehicle and every artillery piece during the war may like this, but I sure don't, and I've read numerous books about WW2. This is just tedious and overly comlpex. YMMV.

UPDATE: 12/17/2021: Having played it for several more hours I finally learned enough to beat the game. I had to not only RTFM (over 200 pages worth!) and play the same scenario a few times until I learned how the HQ system and supply really works, and it is a requirement to use a minimum of core things, like initial bombing of airports; maintaining supply 100% of the time if possible; ability to move units that are out of supply to different HQ units, etc. These are not intuitive skills but essential to beat the game on easy difficulty, and only learned through repetition - i.e. to win, you must prepare to lose a few times, and to learn the esoteric rules. If you find all that rewarding and interesting, then this may be the game for you.

The benchmark all other grand campaign wargames should be compared by. The slavish devotion to historical detail, the expansiveness of the campaigns, the statistical data and battle reporting make this an incredible achievement considering the vastness of scale. It has flaws, but the sheer richness of gameplay more than compensates. This game series, (and the upcoming WitE2,) likely will be the closest we see to having a game like Europa come to fruition on PC. Is it expensive? Yes, and rightfully so. If you have played tabletop wargames before, you know there is a small, but dedicated following. These games will never achieve mass appeal, and therefore are supported by diehards with the cost of production very high and development taking years, if not decades in some instances. The price is comparable to those games, and often cheaper (Compared with say ADG's World in Flames.) This isn't a one-and-done game, it is a major time commitment both to learn how to play, then to execute the turns. With one turn easily taking an hour or longer, over 100 turns means one game alone can take weeks to complete (esp if playing PBEM.) You get your money's worth.
Strongly recommend a purchase if you have devoted considerable time as a board wargamer, and if you don't mind pouring over a few hundred pages of instructions (there is a quick start guide though so don't be too put off.) If you like grand strategy games like HOI4, etc that allow for considerable ahistorical gameplay, you may not necessarily like this one. In that case (and anyone on the fence about it,) I'd recommend watching some Let's Plays on Youtube to see if it's right for you.

Upon it's release 11 years ago, it was truly something special given its complete database of units and weapons on such a grand scale and perhaps, like WITE2, one could justify its cost then, especially to the grognards. This game is great to recreate the conflict but not if you want to try alternatives. What I dislike about this game is the inability to allow some good 'what if' situations/scenarios plus the Editor is absolutely awful. However, I get it - realism. Anyway, it's good for a while but for me, I lost interest after fighting the good fight knowing what was causing my failures but not being able to change them. For example, what if instead Barbarossa started in April instead of June? What if the weather was better or more supply was getting through or the main push was South instead of Central, Moscow? Perhaps WITE2 is a better game but I hear it really isn't much different. I cannot recommend its purchase unless you get it on a good sale.
